title: A1 — Paddles Up
snippet: Sharpen crew unison — every paddle at the same height, entering the water on the same instant, on command.

title: A2 — In Together, Out Together
snippet: The foundational same-side synchronization drill — every blade enters and exits the water at the exact same instant, all session, every session.

title: A3 — Pause-at-the-Back Drill
snippet: Teach the crew to feel and honor the canoe's natural glide by pausing briefly at the back of the stroke (never the front), which avoids "boat dive" and unweighting the glide.

title: A4 — Eyes-Closed Timing Drill
snippet: Advanced synchronization test — keep perfect time using only the boat's rhythm and the sound of other blades, no visual cues.

title: A5 — Chalk Talks
snippet: Use brief on-land walkthroughs to correct a specific technical fault the whole crew shares, without burning water time on explanation.

title: B6 — The Va'a Stroke Phase Drill
snippet: Teach the three-phase stroke (Catch → Pull → Push) as distinct, progressive efforts rather than one uniform pull, so paddlers stop "spending their power at the front."

title: B7 — BBB — Blade Before Butt
snippet: Fix the common fault of dumping body weight straight down into the seat instead of engaging the blade and feet first to build tension through the kinetic chain.

title: B8 — Return / Relax-Wrist Drill
snippet: Smooth out rushed, choppy paddle returns by teaching paddlers to relax the wrists at the finish and swing the paddle back in a controlled half-circle close to the water.

title: B9 — Common-Mistakes Self-Check Drill
snippet: Give each paddler a structured way to self-diagnose their own technical fault from a known checklist, rather than waiting for a coach to spot it.

title: B10 — Pull-Not-Push Mental Model (Land Cue)
snippet: Land-based teaching concept — the canoe is pulled forward to the paddle (like a mountaineer's ice axe anchor), not pushed — corrects the tendency to enter too far back and stroke too long.

title: B11 — Video / Skiff Critique Sessions
snippet: Use footage of the crew's own stroke to make technical feedback concrete instead of abstract.

title: C12 — Build-Then-Burst Bump Drill
category: Drill · Catching Waves / Surfing the Bump
snippet: Train the rate change needed to catch a wave/wake/bump — build for several strokes, then spike rate and get "up front" with the paddle to catch it, then settle into deep power strokes once caught.

title: C13 — Opening-Scouting Drill
category: Drill · Catching Waves / Surfing the Bump
snippet: Practice identifying a usable "opening" in a wave/wake ahead — dead ahead or off to the side — and calling the right response to reach it.

title: C14 — Energy-Balance Drill
category: Drill · Catching Waves / Surfing the Bump
snippet: Teach the "just enough, not too much" feel of holding a wave or wake without dropping into the trough behind it — a feel-based drill, not a mechanical one.

title: D15 — Ladders
snippet: Build both fitness and rate-control by paddling structured time-based "rungs" at increasing then decreasing duration.

title: D16 — Pyramid Interval
snippet: A specific ladder variant — ascend and descend through a full range of efforts in one continuous set, finishing with a maximal push.

title: D17 — Heavy-Blade / Resistance Work
snippet: Build raw stroke strength by adding resistance — a larger/heavier blade, a bungee cord around the hull, or water loaded into the canoe — while paddling at a controlled, slow rate.

title: D18 — Power-10 Burst Set
snippet: A short, explosive burst set adapted from the ladder/pyramid principle — a natural fit as a race-simulation power piece, borrowed from rowing's "Power 10."

title: D19 — Stroke-Rate Change Drills
snippet: Teach the crew to shift stroke rate together, as a unit, rather than each paddler drifting to their own preferred cadence.

title: E20 — Standard Call-and-Switch
snippet: Establish the basic, reliable change mechanic the rest of the changeover drills build on.

title: E21 — Tepava's 4-Step Change Sequence
snippet: Give paddlers a clear internal sequence for a clean change: finish → release → lift & control → higher catch.

title: E22 — On-Land Side-Switch Progression
snippet: Break the changeover down into an isolated land drill for paddlers who need to feel the mechanics without the complexity of being on the water.

title: E23 — Quick Changes Drill
snippet: Drill clean, fast switches under a much higher change frequency than race pace, so normal-paced changes feel easy by comparison.

title: E24 — Fast-Change Drill (Count-Based Variant)
snippet: A close variant of E23 — change sides on a simple stroke count (3–5) rather than a caller's verbal cue, building a more automatic internal sense of timing.

title: E25 — Silent-Call Drill
snippet: Practice changes and general crew communication without verbal calls — useful for sneaking up on or passing another canoe in a race, and sharpens non-verbal crew awareness generally.

title: F26 — Race-Start Drill
snippet: Practice getting the canoe up to full speed quickly after just one side of strokes, simulating an actual race start.

title: F27 — Rabbit Drill
snippet: Build competitive intensity and teach the crew to hold form under pressure by chasing down and passing another canoe.

title: F28 — Close-Quarters Drill
snippet: Build comfort and safety awareness for paddling with other canoes close by, as happens in real race situations (buoy turns, passing, crowded starts).

title: F29 — Turn Drills
snippet: Practice making turns as tight and quick as possible, pairing steering technique with crew-side power management.

title: F30 — Stay-Together Drill
snippet: Practice pacing by having the lead boat deliberately reduce power to stay paired with a following boat — useful for coaching two crews simultaneously or building pacing awareness.

title: G31 — Draw Stroke Practice
snippet: Build steering precision through both active draw strokes and static draws ("posts"), emphasizing frequent small corrections over large, disruptive ones.

title: G32 — Steersman Scenario Training
snippet: Build the steersperson's ability to read conditions and make sound go/no-go and course decisions — a classroom-style session as much as an on-water drill.

title: H33 — Full Huli Recovery Drill
snippet: The mandatory, most important safety drill in the plan — every paddler knows their seat's job the instant a capsize happens, and the crew can right the boat, re-board, and resume in well under a minute. Run at minimum once a year per most racing associations.

title: H34 — Huli-in-Rough-Conditions Drill
snippet: Address the specific gap that most crews only ever practice hulis in calm water, when real capsizes are more likely in wind and chop — this drill closes that gap deliberately.

title: H35 — Boat-Up / Re-Boarding Drill
snippet: Practice getting back into the canoe — solo or as a group — independent of a full huli scenario. A quicker, lower-stakes drill than H33, good for a pool or dock session.

title: H36 — Pre-Launch Safety Brief
snippet: A short, constant ritual — not a full drill — that keeps huli responsibilities fresh in everyone's mind every single time the crew launches.

title: I37 — Positive-Only Calls Rule
snippet: Establish a team norm that keeps the boat a supportive, focused environment — no venting or blame on the water — which in turn keeps technical drills effective instead of turning into finger-pointing.

title: I38 — Session-Intention Drill
snippet: Have each paddler enter every practice with one specific, personal correction in mind, rather than paddling on autopilot.

title: I39 — Boat Familiarity Rule
snippet: Ensure technique work actually transfers to race day by practicing in the same hull/class the crew will actually race, whenever possible.

title: J40 — Catching a Bump — Seat by Seat
snippet: Give every paddler, not just the steersperson, a clear picture of their specific seat's job during a bump catch — including who's actually best positioned to feel it coming and make the call.

title: Boat Orientation Walkthrough
snippet: Give a brand-new paddler the vocabulary and physical layout knowledge needed before anything else makes sense.

title: Instant-Command Recognition Drill
snippet: Every paddler responds to the five core commands instantly and correctly, without having to think about what they mean.

title: Seat Roles Walkthrough & Rotation
snippet: Every paddler understands, at a basic level, what every seat does — not just their own.

title: Basic Right-of-Way Awareness (Crew-Level)
snippet: Every paddler — not just the steersperson — has basic situational awareness of other traffic, even though the steersperson makes the actual navigation calls.

title: Wave Tuck Position Drill
snippet: Train seats 1 and 2 in particular (most exposed to head-on wave impact) to tuck/lean forward into heavy water rather than letting the spine snap backward.

title: First Huli Exposure (Solo, Calm Water)
snippet: Before ever doing a full-crew huli drill, a brand-new paddler should be comfortable and calm capsizing and getting back into a canoe solo, in controlled, shallow, calm conditions.

title: Steersperson Development Path
snippet: Give experienced paddlers a structured path toward steering — including the actual accreditation most will eventually need for racing.

title: Right-of-Way Scenario Drills (Steersperson-Level)
snippet: Take the crew-level awareness from NP4 to the real, steersperson-level skill of making correct right-of-way calls under actual traffic conditions.

title: Full Huli Mastery & Rotation
snippet: Keep the full-crew huli recovery sharp for veterans, including comfort in roles they don't normally paddle.

title: Mentoring Rotation
snippet: Use veteran experience deliberately to bring new paddlers up to speed faster, rather than leaving it to chance.

title: Pre-Practice Warm-Up / Post-Practice Cooldown Routine
snippet: Cut shoulder-strain and low-back injury risk and help the crew sync up faster, using a dynamic warm-up / static cooldown routine done together as a crew.

title: Hydration & Fueling Protocol
snippet: Keep every paddler fueled and hydrated enough to hold power and timing through a full practice or a multi-heat Nine-Man race day, and recognize/react to heat-related emergencies before they become serious.

title: Draw Stroke Practice
snippet: Build steering precision through both active draw strokes and static draws ("posts"), emphasizing frequent small corrections over large, disruptive ones.

title: Steersman Scenario Training
snippet: Build the steersperson's ability to read conditions and make sound go/no-go and course decisions — a classroom-style session as much as an on-water drill.

title: Lineup & Boat Balance
snippet: Give the steersperson a practical framework for assigning seats so the canoe balances well before it ever leaves the dock — cutting down on corrections that are really a lineup problem wearing a conditions costume.

title: Poke-Count Awareness Drill
snippet: Train a steersperson to correct drift primarily by paddle-steering (adjusting their own stroke) rather than by ruddering — every poke of the blade as a brake costs speed, even in water that looks flat.

title: Hull Weight & Response — Coaching Discussion
snippet: Give a steersperson and coaching staff a shared, accurate mental model for what hull weight and shape actually change, so hull choice is matched to the steersperson and conditions rather than defaulting to “lighter is always faster.”

title: Rhumb-Line Discipline Drill
snippet: Build the habit of tracking deliberate departures from the direct course line — chasing speed (bumps, favorable current) is fine, but only when the steersperson can say how far off line they are and whether it's paying for itself.

title: Tactical Composure Through a Water Change
snippet: Layer race-tactics awareness on top of already-solid changeover mechanics — the real time gain in a change comes from a calm, fast entry into it, not just a quick physical swap.

title: Confidence & Composure Under Pressure
snippet: Build the calm, unpanicked response that separates elite crews under pressure — a rival's surge, a gear hiccup, an imperfect change — treated as information to process, not a crisis to react to.

title: Steersperson Development Path
snippet: Give experienced paddlers a structured path toward steering — including the actual accreditation most will eventually need for racing.

title: Right-of-Way Scenario Drills (Steersperson-Level)
snippet: Take basic crew-level right-of-way awareness to the real, steersperson-level skill of making correct calls under actual traffic conditions.

title: Dry-Land / Dock Change Walkthrough
snippet: Teach the full sequence of calls, hand signals, and body positioning with zero water risk, before ever doing it live.

title: Calm-Water Single-Swimmer Change Drill
snippet: Build the individual entry skill — signal, positioning, grab, front support, seated — one paddler at a time, isolated from the complexity of a full crew rotation.

title: Full-Crew Change Rotation Drill
snippet: Run the complete water-change sequence with a full crew and a real escort boat, including calling, ama-side positioning, and (if applicable) skirt unzip/zip — the actual race scenario.

title: Escort Boat Skipper Briefing (Standing Pre-Race Practice)
snippet: Make steersperson/coach-to-skipper coordination a habit, not a one-off — the single lowest-effort, highest-payoff item on this page.

title: Mental Visualization Practice
snippet: Build the “autopilot” a fast, calm water change runs on through off-water mental rehearsal — genuinely part of how elite crews report mastering changes, not a soft add-on.

title: In the Water (Paddler About to Get In)
snippet: After leaving the escort boat, line up in seat order in the water with appropriate spacing from the next paddler.

title: In the Canoe (Before a Change)
snippet: The caller repositions paddlers so whoever is about to get out is paddling on the ama side — this keeps their blade and body out of the way of paddlers coming in, and lets paddlers staying in keep paddling hard without dodging bodies. (Works best for 1-2 person changes; for a 3-person change, one paddler staying in can shift to ama side once the incoming bodies have passed.)

title: The Approach and Grab (Entering Paddler)
snippet: Left hand makes light contact with the side of the canoe as it arrives — this is for proprioception, so your body knows where the canoe is by touch as much as sight.

title: Getting Out (Exiting Paddler)
snippet: Timing: stow your paddle when your replacement is about 2-3 seats away. Exit the canoe when they're about 1-2 seats away.

title: Sprayskirts — Clearing Up a Common Misconception
snippet: A fully unzipped sprayskirt gives more room to get in, not less, and better traction than a bare, often-waxed gunwale.

title: Seat 1 — The Stroker
snippet: Every other seat is reacting to Seat 1 — the entire crew's rhythm, rate, and technique flow from this seat. If it falters here, the whole canoe suffers. It's not a power seat, but it's psychologically demanding: paddling out front, self-motivated, with nobody's stroke to follow but your own feel for the boat.

title: Seat 2
snippet: The other half of the pace-setting pair — and arguably the more technically demanding seat of the two, since Seat 2 has no blade ahead of them to visually follow. Matching Seat 1's rhythm by feel alone, stroke after stroke, is a genuinely underrated skill. Miss a change here and the whole crew goes out of time.

title: Seat 3
snippet: The start of the engine room — and in most crews, the caller. A center seat gets the most stable, least wave-affected connection to the water of any position in the boat, which is exactly why it's trusted to put down serious, consistent power without disturbing the steersperson's line.

title: Seat 4
snippet: The other half of the engine room — a pure power position that builds on the foundation Seats 1 and 2 set up front. This is generally a seat for a strong, heavier paddler who can hold serious output deep into a race.

title: Seat 5
snippet: Part power seat, part steersperson support — often used as a training seat for newer paddlers, but a genuinely strong Seat 5 can transform a crew. This is the bridge between the engine room and the steering, handling the roughest water in the boat while staying in constant communication with Seat 6.

title: Seat 6 — Steersperson & Captain
snippet: First responsibility: crew safety. Second: canoe safety. Third: steering and navigation — in that order. Every other seat defers to Seat 6's call in any safety situation, no exceptions. This seat carries more depth than fits on one card here; the full steering skillset — draw strokes, race-craft, accreditation — has its own dedicated page.

title: Ama
snippet: The outrigger float, connected to the main hull by the iako. What keeps an outrigger canoe from tipping over sideways — and the side you always re-board from after a huli.

title: Attack Distance
snippet: The proper distance range for an entering paddler to be from the canoe as it arrives during a water change — no more than an arm's length away, no less than a foot.

title: Bump
snippet: A wave or wake a canoe can catch and ride for extra speed, similar to surfing. Elite crews read several bumps ahead rather than catching whatever's directly in front of them.

title: Carry
snippet: The momentum a hull holds onto once it's moving. A heavier hull has more carry — it holds speed through a bump longer once caught — but takes longer to build that speed in the first place.

title: Changeover
snippet: The crew switching paddling sides together, called by “Hut,” executed on the recovery phase of the next stroke so the boat never loses rhythm or speed. Also just called a “change.”

title: Draw Stroke
snippet: An active steering stroke that pulls the stern toward the paddle side — used for a stronger, more deliberate correction than a post.

title: Engine Room
snippet: Seats 3, 4, and 5 collectively — the crew's primary power source, positioned centrally enough in the hull to deliver sustained output without disturbing the steersperson's line.

title: Escort Boat
snippet: The support boat in a Nine-Man race carrying the 3 paddlers not currently in the canoe, plus hydration, food, and safety gear. Its skipper is making real-time navigation and safety calls the entire race.

title: Front Support Position
snippet: The body position immediately after grabbing the canoe during a water change — both hands and the hip line on the gunwale, weight on the hands — right before swinging the legs in and getting seated.

title: Huli
snippet: A capsize — the canoe flipping over. Also used as a verb (“we hulied”) and as the name for the recovery drill every crew practices to right the canoe and re-board.

title: Hut
snippet: The verbal call for a changeover, given one stroke before the crew actually switches sides — not an instruction to switch immediately.

title: Hyponatremia
snippet: A dangerously low blood-sodium level caused by drinking too much plain water without replacing electrolytes — signs include nausea, headache, confusion, and swelling. Treated with electrolytes, never more plain water.

title: Iako
snippet: The crossbeams (booms) connecting the main hull to the ama. Also where a spare steering paddle is typically strapped for quick access.

title: Kūpuna
snippet: Hawaiian word for elders — often invoked as the source of traditional canoe-building knowledge and paddling customs passed down through generations.

title: Mana
snippet: Spiritual power or life force. In Hawaiian tradition, a canoe itself is believed to carry mana — part of why it's treated as a crewmate, not equipment.

title: Manu
snippet: The carved, bird-like piece at the bow and/or stern of a traditional canoe.

title: Momoa
snippet: A small, otherwise unexplained flat spot at the stern of a traditional canoe — by tradition, the seat for the canoe's own protective spirit. See the History & Tradition section on the Fundamentals page for the full story.

title: Nine-Man
snippet: A long-distance racing format: 9 total paddlers, 6 paddling the canoe at any moment and 3 riding an escort boat, rotating in and out via water changes without the canoe ever stopping. Most SCORA long-distance races, including the Catalina Crossing, are run this way.

title: OC6
snippet: An outrigger canoe paddled by six people — the boat class this entire site is about. (An OC1 is the single-paddler version, an OC9 the nine-person escort-boat racing configuration.)

title: Overlap
snippet: A right-of-way concept at a turn or mark: whichever canoe has established overlap (bow within the zone) generally has the right of way. Also used more loosely for how far a steersperson has drifted off the direct course line.

title: Poke
snippet: A quick steering correction made by planting the blade flat against the side of the hull — typically by seat 6 or seat 1 — and levering off it to turn the boat. Faster and more reflexive than a full draw stroke, but it still acts as a brake, so the best steerspeople keep pokes short, rare, and caught early.

title: Post
snippet: A static draw: holding the blade planted at an angle without taking a full stroke, letting the boat's forward motion do the turning work. A subtler, more continuous correction than a full draw stroke.

title: Rhumb Line
snippet: A real nautical term for a straight course of constant compass bearing, pronounced “rum line” — in racing, the direct reference course a steersperson tracks deliberate detours against (chasing a bump, favorable current) to judge whether the detour is actually paying for itself.

title: Rocker
snippet: The curvature of a hull from bow to stern. More rocker makes a hull turn more easily but track less predictably in a straight line; less rocker holds a line well but is harder to turn.

title: Sprayskirt (Skirt)
snippet: A cover over the canoe's cockpit openings that keeps water out. Unzipped back-to-front before a water change and re-zipped front-to-back after, one seat at a time.

title: Steersperson (Steersman)
snippet: The paddler in seat 6, responsible for steering and holding final say on safety decisions in the canoe. “Steersman” is the older/traditional term for the same role.

title: Trim
snippet: How a canoe's weight is balanced front-to-back. Poor trim changes how the bow rides and can affect how the hull handles chop or catches a bump — a lineup consideration alongside side-to-side power balance.

title: Vaʻa (Waʻa)
snippet: Hawaiian word for canoe — spelled vaʻa or waʻa depending on dialect/source. “Vaʻa stroke” refers to the traditional outrigger paddling stroke.

title: Water Change
snippet: A paddler swap during Nine-Man racing where one paddler physically exits into the ocean and another enters, while the canoe keeps moving at speed — a completely different event from a Hut changeover, where everyone stays seated.

title: Wave Tuck
snippet: Leaning forward into an oncoming wave to protect the spine, rather than staying upright or leaning back into the impact. Seats 1 and 2 take the brunt of it and benefit most from the habit.
